key_points: S. N. Aiyer's "Disturbing Trends" protests the arrest of three anti-communist workers under the Defence of India Rules even as it endorses banning the Communist Party outright, and warns that V. K. Krishna Menon's call for a "one nation, one policy, one leader" cult and the AICC's branding of criticism of Nehru as treason mark a slide toward authoritarianism.

Raman Desai's "Financing The War" argues India's roughly Rs. 1000-crore annual defence bill can only be met through mass savings from ordinary peasants and workers rather than a narrow income-tax base, and calls for a more equalitarian, US-style economy and an independent Planning Commission.

The reprinted "Open Letter To Members Of Parliament" by Dharampal, Roop Narain and N. N. Datta, the three men arrested for criticising Nehru, insists that criticism of the Prime Minister is a democratic right and no less patriotic than support for the government.

S. R. Mohan Das's "Cease Fire Or War By 'Other Means'?" argues, citing M. N. Roy's 1951 warnings on Tibet and Lenin's writings on deceiving the West, that the Chinese cease-fire is not peace but a shift to diplomatic and psychological pressure on India.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Non-Alignment Plus" and Devadas Kini's "God That Failed" both argue non-alignment was undermined by illusory trust in Communist China and Soviet neutrality, with Kini calling it a failed 'religion' and urging India to recognise its natural bonds with the democratic West.

A translated reprint from the Uruguayan journal El Plata, "An Instructive Reality," cites India's post-invasion predicament as proof that neutralism sympathetic to Communism is self-defeating and warns Uruguayan politicians against romanticising it.

A joint statement by Calcutta intellectuals welcomes Indo-Pakistan talks and urges both governments to compromise on Kashmir so as to present a united front against Chinese domination of the subcontinent.

The issue's "With Many Voices" column of quotations includes Indira Gandhi asserting Congress unity exists only 'behind my father' and N. G. Ranga declaring in Parliament that Nehru 'should have been dismissed long ago.'

M. R. Masani's "When Not To Negotiate" opposes any negotiation with China before full withdrawal from territory held since 1947/1950, invoking Parliament's unanimous 14 November resolution and Rajaji's warning that the Colombo Proposals would make India a permanent satellite of China.

An unsigned editorial criticises Nehru's claim that government need not constantly refer back to Parliament, warning that a Cabinet answerable only to a regimented majority risks becoming 'a disguised dictatorship.'

Zbigniew Brzezinski's contribution analyses the Cuban missile crisis as a decisive setback for Soviet claims of a shifted balance of power, and frames China's attack on India as part of a bid for regional primacy that would isolate India from its neighbours.

Robert S. Elegant's "As Others See Us" reprint dismantles the 'myth' of Nehru's India as a major independent force in world affairs, citing his foreign-policy inconsistencies and arguing Indian diplomacy has actually abetted Communist gains in Indochina.

A. G. Noorani's piece critiques a government study defending the proposal to fold the Attorney-General's office into the Law Ministry, arguing the Constituent Assembly deliberately rejected such a merger and that the office's independence protects impartial legal advice.

M. A. Venkata Rao's piece reads the Chinese NEFA offensive as following the classic pattern of Communist unconventional warfare seen in Telangana and Kerala, and proposes a 50,000-strong volunteer frontier guard for propaganda counter-work and vigilance.

M. Devadas Kini's piece surveys rival theories of Chinese intentions and concludes China's aim is simply to dominate Asia, arguing India needs a sustained Western military alliance rather than temporary aid.

The issue reprints Patrick Henry's 1775 'Give me liberty or give me death' speech as, in the editors' framing, prophetic of India's predicament vis-a-vis China, and closes with a 'With Many Voices' column quoting Frank Moraes's criticism of the Colombo Formula as favouring the aggressor.

Raman Desai's "Defence In The Air" argues India's air defence has been dangerously neglected, invoking Normandy and Korea to insist wars are won by offensive air power, and calls for alliance with 'tried friends' rather than boundary concessions to China.
A short piece on "The Peacock" reflects on India's national emblem, paired with James McAuley's reprinted poem "Innocent By Definition" satirising morally evasive political rhetoric.

S. Sharangpani's account of the Third Afro-Asian Solidarity Conference at Moshi describes how the Indian delegation was outmanoeuvred into a resolution favourable to China, with delegation leader Chaman Lal admitting "we were double-crossed."

An "As Others See Us" reprint from the American National Review argues China's consolidation of Tibet lets it squeeze Bhutan, Sikkim and Nepal, criticises V. K. Krishna Menon's pro-Communist influence, and still urges continued Western military aid to India.

Adam Adil's "Dr. Sukarno And Malaysia" condemns Indonesian President Sukarno's opposition to the proposed Malaysian Federation as 'neo Afro-Asian imperialism' serving Soviet and Chinese interests, and argues India should support Malaysia as a check on Communism in Southeast Asia.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "De-Militarisation Of Tibet" traces treaty history including the 1914 McMahon Line to argue India's 1950-51 acquiescence in China's absorption of Tibet was a moral and strategic error, and calls for Tibet's de-militarisation backed by a Western defence pact.

Dr. L. M. Singhvi, M.P., in "Emergency And Government," defends the constitutional propriety of the Defence of India Act, citing Constituent Assembly debates, while calling for parliamentary vigilance against abuse of emergency powers.

M. Devadas Kini's "Reluctant Nationalists?" traces the CPI's shifting, Moscow-aligned positions on the Sino-Indian dispute from 1930 to 1962, concluding that "a genuine communist cannot be a genuine nationalist."

The issue closes with a review of Aderogba Ajao's memoir "Six Years Under Communism" on forced detention in East Germany, a Laxman cartoon, and a "With Many Voices" column quoting C. Rajagopalachari comparing debate over Western alignment to "discussing vegetarianism in a Chinese restaurant."

S. Natarajan's "Emergency And The Press" argues no genuine press emergency justifies the revived Defence of India Rules, tracing a history of successful press self-regulation and criticising Nehru's claim that press freedom is compromised chiefly by "the power of money."

M. R. Masani's "A Lethal Budget" denounces the Super Profits Tax as an attack on joint-stock enterprise dressed up as a defence measure, defending free enterprise via Gandhi's trusteeship concept and Ludwig Erhard's "Social Enterprise."

Raman K. Desai's "This World Of Murky Business" surveys the Vivian Bose Commission's findings against the Tatas, Mafatlal and Ambica Mills, and warns that government hypocrisy and business malpractice together risk pushing India toward communism or military dictatorship.

V. B. Karnik's "The Myth Of Non-Alignment" argues the Chinese invasion exposed non-alignment as a pragmatic policy rather than a moral principle, since India rushed to accept Western arms once China attacked.
Harvard professor Samuel P. Huntington's "Alliances And Tensions" analyses the shift from a bipolar to a diffuse, multipolar world order and the fraying of both the Sino-Soviet and Atlantic blocs.

M. R. Pai's "The Perquisitive Society" documents lavish government perquisites, including Union Ministers' average monthly water and electricity bills of Rs. 13,489, and calls for their elimination in favour of transparent, adequately paid public service.

Adam Adil's "Fate Of Muslims In Communist China" reports on the repression of China's roughly sixty million Muslims, including closed schools, suppressed Arabic instruction, and continuing revolt in Sinkiang.
The issue closes with a "With Many Voices" digest and the statutory Statement About Ownership naming Adam Adil as printer/publisher and Raman K. Desai as editor.

V. B. Karnik's "Security And Public Services" defends a Bihar circular barring Communists from rifle training, citing Britain's 1962 Radcliffe Commission on Communist penetration of civil-service unions to argue India, now "at war with a communist Power," should screen Communists from security-sensitive posts.

S. Natarajan's "Individual Liberty And The Law" criticises the Home Ministry's handling of the Defence of India Rules detentions of taxi-union leaders George Fernandes and Janardhan Upadhye, and Home Minister Lal Bahadur Sastri's practice of settling civil-liberties disputes in private rather than before Parliament.

Roman O. Zybenko's "Failure Of Gold Control In Russia" draws on Soviet press reports of gold-theft rings and black-market networks to argue the Soviet state's gold monopoly is riddled with corruption despite the death penalty for currency speculation.

A. B. Shah's "The Spirit Of Lincoln" reads Lincoln's containment of slavery, and his refusal to suspend civil liberties or elections during the Civil War, as a model applicable to India's confrontation with Communist China.

A piece on the 1961 CPSU programme argues that despite its rhetoric of peaceful coexistence, the programme still commits Communist parties to "all forms of struggle, peaceful and non-peaceful," and that the Khrushchev-Mao split is tactical rather than a real break with the goal of world revolution.
Rama Swarup Sabherwal's survey of Ceylon argues that despite Communists' poor electoral record there, the real danger lies in infiltration of trade unions, the civil service and front organisations.

Kamalashanker Pandya's report on the Dohad by-election credits the Swatantra Party's tripled winning margin in Gujarat's Dohad by-election to a broad anti-Congress alliance and rising awareness of Chinese aggression.

S. P. Aiyar reviews A. Doak Barnett's "Communist China and Asia," praising its account of Chinese strategic thinking and its argument that Peking's 1962 attack on India aimed partly to show South-East Asia that Indian non-alignment was, in practice, aligned with the West.

V. B. Karnik's "A Challenge To Mr. Nehru" reads Acharya Kripalani's and Dr. Lohia's by-election wins at Amroha and Farrukhabad as a direct popular rebuke of Nehru, noting Congress ran a covertly communal campaign and that Communists actively campaigned for Congress against Kripalani.

A press-reactions digest, "Amroha And Farrukhabad," collects newspaper reactions ranging from the Indian Express calling the Amroha result a "resounding slap" at Nehru to Patriot dissenting that the results were a win for reactionary, communal and capitalist forces.

Raman Desai's "Suppression Of News" argues Indian newspapers gave the damning Vivian Bose Commission report on the Dalmia-Jain group only cursory coverage while giving a rebuttal from one of the accused disproportionate space, warning that commercial capture threatens the press's inherited moral standing.

Rama Swarup Sabherwal describes South Vietnam's Strategic Hamlet Scheme, launched March 1962, as a counter-insurgency and nation-building programme meant to deny the Viet Cong a rural base while decentralising local administration.

M. R. Pai's "Corruption In Public Life" surveys the Dalmia-Jain and Malaviya-Sirajuddin scandals, criticises Nehru for accepting a commemorative volume from a businessman under Bose Commission investigation, and calls for simplified company law and reduced state discretion as the real check on corruption.

An unsigned editorial, "Tortuous Foreign Policy," criticises Nehru for praising Nasser's Arab Unity declaration while treating Israel coldly and Malaysia's Tunku Abdul Rahman lukewarmly, arguing fifteen years of non-alignment have alienated India's natural democratic allies.

Adam Adil's "Sino-Soviet Conflict" argues the China-USSR rift is a "family quarrel" within a still-united Communist bloc driven by personal rivalry between Mao and Khrushchev, not doctrine, and warns that Western hopes of exploiting the split are illusory.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "India's Tradition In Foreign Policy" rejects Nehru's panchsheel as rooted in Indian spiritual tradition, arguing the true classical tradition is Chanakya's realist mandala system of calculated alliances and vigilance.
Aamir Ali reviews Alexander Solzhenitsyn's "One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich," praising its unmelodramatic realism and situating its publication as a landmark of Khrushchev-era liberalisation.

The issue closes with "With Many Voices," quoting Nehru calling communists "100 per cent patriots" and Dr. Lohia defining communism as "Socialism, minus democracy, plus centralization, plus civil war, plus Russia."

V. B. Karnik's "The Opposition And Its Task" argues that although by-election wins in Amroha, Farrukhabad and Rajkot have fuelled demand for a united opposition, full merger is unrealistic; he calls instead for ad hoc electoral cooperation among parties against Congress's corrupt, weak administration.

Raman Desai's "U.N. Finances" surveys the United Nations' financial crisis, detailing the Soviet Bloc's, France's and Belgium's refusal to pay Congo and Gaza peacekeeping costs, and urges India to press for enforcement of Assembly payment rules against defaulters.

Yogindra Trivedi's "Compulsory Deposit Scheme" examines the new Act's mechanics and constitutional validity, flagging the absence of any appellate authority and a timing lacuna, and concludes its administrative burden outweighs its dubious social benefit.

Peter Ritner's "The Battle Of Clay's Cliches" defends the U.S. Clay Report's aim of fostering pluralist, entrepreneurial societies through aid, proposing that assistance shift from mega infrastructure projects toward small, closely supervised private ventures concentrated on pivotal states like India, Brazil and Nigeria.

M. D. Kini's "Mr. Dange And China" dissects CPI leader S. A. Dange's pamphlet defending Congress's China policy, arguing Dange's support was survival tactics justified in Marxist rather than nationalist terms, and highlighting his disclosure that India had reportedly considered surrendering the Aksai Chin road.

An unsigned report on the "British Press Council" covers its adoption of a revised constitution with a lay chairman and trimmed objectives following the 1961-62 Royal Commission on the Press, with an accompanying editorial questioning whether the reform risks drifting toward censorship.

The "Without Comment" column reprints items on Communist-bloc arms sales to apartheid South Africa and alleged Soviet secrecy over cosmonaut deaths, plus a note on Chinese propaganda urging patients to rely on "revolutionary optimism" over medicine.
The issue closes with "With Many Voices," compiling reactions to Minoo Masani's Rajkot win and three separate Arthur Koestler quotations from Encounter on Bertrand Russell and British decline.

M. R. Masani's "The Evolution Of An Opposition" traces India's weak opposition to Congress absorbing independent political currents after independence, and endorses ad hoc "unity in action" among opposition parties rather than formal merger, citing wins at Dohad, Amroha, Farrukhabad and Rajkot.

Pheroze J. Shroff's "Corruption: Causes And Cure" blames endemic corruption on the licence-permit regime's discretionary power and on inflationary finance debasing public morals, calling for dismantling controls alongside asset disclosure and vigilance committees.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "Powers Of The President" rebuts K. M. Munshi's claim that the President can override the Council of Ministers, working through Articles 52-78 and Walter Bagehot's formula for constitutional monarchy to conclude the President's real influence is limited to being informed, consulted, and to warn.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Today's Reformation In India" reinterprets the Bhagavad Gita's teaching of equal divinity across all beings and its ethic of public-spirited action as scriptural grounding for a modern reformation supporting democracy and equality of opportunity.

An unsigned editorial, "Guilt Complex At Work," criticises the government's evasive, defensive public statement on the joint Indo-US-UK air exercises, arguing appeasement of non-alignment purists undercuts India's ability to build real defence capacity against China.

Soviet defector Aleksandr Kaznacheev's "Why Sino-Soviet Conflict?" argues the Sino-Soviet split is structural rather than ideological, since both regimes depend on an external enemy to justify dictatorship at home, and compares Mao's China to Hitler's Germany.

V. B. Karnik reviews Kaznacheev's memoir "Inside a Soviet Embassy," detailing how the Rangoon embassy functioned as a subversion operation, including a fabricated bribery story planted against Morarji Desai.
A review of "China Invades India," edited by Karnik, singles out contributor B. K. Desai's charge that Nehru was prepared to concede Tibet to China even before his 1949 Peking visit.
The issue closes with "With Many Voices," including Macmillan's remark on the Profumo scandal ("two tarts") and Sukarno's comment on not wanting to be told he is wrong.

Raman Desai's "An Invitation To Autocracy" condemns Nehru's removal of six Central Ministers and six Chief Ministers under the Kamaraj Plan, especially Finance Minister Morarji Desai, warning it concentrates unchecked, dictatorial power in Nehru's hands and comparing his foreign policy of appeasement to Chamberlain's toward Nazi Germany.

Raman Desai's second piece, "The Berlin Wall," marks the wall's second anniversary with statistics on its scale and toll -- 27 miles, 129 watch towers, 65 people killed attempting to cross -- and the mass exodus of nearly 4 million East Germans before its construction.

M. R. Masani's "Socialism Or State Capitalism?", extracted from his No-Confidence Motion speech, argues fifteen years of professed socialism have produced a "New Class" of politicians, officials and cronies while real wages for labour and peasants stagnated, citing a 370-step bureaucratic land-allotment process and the perverse Gold Control Order.

V. B. Karnik's "Bombay Civic Strike - An Evaluation" reviews the collapse of the Municipal Mazdoor Union's dearness-allowance strike, faulting the union for escalating without exhausting conciliation machinery and the Government for treating the dispute as a political rather than industrial confrontation.

S. R. Mohan Das's "The Kamaraj Plan" traces the plan's origin to the Amroha-Farukhabad-Rajkot by-election defeats and endorses N. V. Gadgil's verdict that the scheme has made the Prime Minister a dictator, however unintentionally.

M. D. Kini's "Split In The Communist Church" surveys the widening Sino-Soviet rupture from Khrushchev's 1956 denunciation of Stalin through the Cuban missile crisis and the Sino-Indian war, asking whether the schism will prove as momentous as the Christian schism five centuries earlier.

The issue's "With Many Voices" column quotes Karl Popper warning that centralised planning inevitably leads to a closed society, and N. V. Gadgil predicting Nehru would be automatically vested with dictatorial powers once his Finance Minister was removed.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's lengthy critique of the "17th Amendment To The Constitution" argues it is a Congress-engineered evasion of judicial review following the Supreme Court's striking down of the Kerala Agrarian Relations Act, warning it opens the door to Soviet- or Chinese-style agricultural collectivisation and threatens millions of ryotwari landholders.

G. L. Mehta's "Private And Public Enterprise," from a FICCI seminar address, argues both sectors have complementary strengths rooted in national character rather than inherent virtue, with the private sector teaching cost discipline and the public sector teaching social responsibility.

Adam Adil's "Malaysia" surveys the newly formed Federation of Malaysia's demographics and economy, attributing Indonesia's "confrontation" policy against it to Chinese Communist pressure on the Indonesian Communist Party and Sukarno's domestic political calculations.

N. S. Ranganath Rao's "The Law Of Obscenity" argues a Bombay bookseller's conviction for importing obscene books without knowledge wrongly dispensed with mens rea, and calls for a specialist board to assess obscenity before customs act.

R. Srinivasan's review of Donald E. Smith's "India as a Secular State" argues Indian government became secular before society developed secular values, citing Congress's own communal compromises in Kerala, Rajkot and Amroha, and the unintended entrenchment of caste consciousness through reservation policy.

The "Without Comment" column reprints an Organiser head-count debunking Communist Party claims about a Delhi "Great March" demonstration's size, and a Mainstream profile sharply critical of General B. M. Kaul's conduct during the 1962 NEFA debacle.

The issue's "With Many Voices" column and closing editorial postscript invoke John Locke's theory of government by consent to argue the 17th Amendment should not pass without a clear electoral mandate.

S. Natarajan's "The Press and The Emergency" argues the wartime-era Press Consultative Committee code, revived amid an undeclared 'emergency,' conscripts editors into suppressing information the government deems prejudicial, and calls for relaxing rather than tightening press restrictions.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "The Denning Report And India" uses Lord Denning's Profumo inquiry to propose that Indian Presidents and Governors be empowered to receive affidavit-based corruption complaints referred to sitting judges, rejecting both a Swedish Ombudsman and a Russian Procurator-General model as unsuited to India.

M. R. Pai's "'Sacred' Steel?" argues India's 'steel first' planning priority, copied from Soviet practice under P. C. Mahalanobis, is economically wasteful given Hindustan Steel's massive cost overruns and losses, and calls for redirecting investment to agriculture and consumer goods.

V. B. Karnik's "The Seventeenth Amendment" rebuts Mulgaonkar's collectivisation fears from an earlier issue, showing the 124 Acts the amendment validates are popularly-mandated tenancy-reform and land-ceiling laws, not Soviet-style collective farming.

Madhu Limaye's "The Civic Strike: Another View" rebuts Karnik's account of the Bombay municipal strike, blaming the Maharashtra government's refusal to negotiate and mass arrests for escalating the dispute, and disputing Karnik's verdict that the strike was a failure.

An unsigned dispatch, "Formosa Today," assesses Nationalist Chinese guerrilla operations against the mainland following the Great Leap Forward's agricultural collapse, and warns that a Nationalist-Communist civil war risks drawing in Soviet intervention rather than restoring Chiang Kai-shek.

K. K. Sinha's "The Jaipur Thesis" critiques the Congress Party's "Democracy and Socialism" thesis, arguing its chain from planning to state ownership and forced cooperativisation will crush the entrepreneurial and middle classes and curtail free elections as the ruling party brands critics "anti-people."

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "The Kairon Enquiry" contrasts Lord Denning's candid Profumo report with Nehru's evasive defence of Punjab Chief Minister Pratap Singh Kairon despite adverse Supreme Court findings against him.

A. B. Shah's "The Radhakrishnan Report" offers an admiring retrospective on the 1949 University Education Commission's recommendations -- capped university size, objective testing, opposition to caste-based reservation -- lamenting that implementation remains partial and distorted.

Raman Desai's "Suppression of Opinion" reports the government's banning of George N. Patterson's "Peking Vs. Delhi" under the Defence of India Rules while Bertrand Russell's similarly critical "Unarmed Victory" went unbanned, accusing Nehru and Nanda of suppressing embarrassing criticism.

The "Without Comment" column rejects Krishna Menon's equating of Chinese and Pakistani "aggression," arguing Pakistan had an arguable claim via the promised Kashmir plebiscite while China's seizure of Tibet had no comparable basis.

Raman Desai reviews the seminar volume "A New Look at Communism" (ed. A. B. Shah and Nissim Ezekiel), praising its argument that resisting communist expansion requires contesting its underlying ideas, not just its territory.

A second review (signed B.K.D.) of The China Quarterly's Formosa survey criticises its anti-Nationalist bias while crediting its articles on Formosa's economic growth and the alienation of Formosan intellectuals toward liberal-democratic ideals.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari arguing it is effectively impossible to prove the corruption of a leader who holds absolute power over witnesses, and Nehru's own remark on having an "emotional rapport" with Marx and Lenin without having read them.

M. R. Masani's Lok Sabha speech on the "Mid-term Appraisal of the Third Plan" quotes the government's own admissions of shortfalls in national income, foodgrains and steel output, calls the Plan an "abject failure," and proposes scrapping it for a consumer-driven mixed economy grounded in Gandhi's talisman of testing policy against its benefit to "the poorest and weakest man."

Raman Desai's "Planning And The Poorest" argues the Planning Commission is merely an advisory body controlled by the Cabinet, and cites government data showing 64% of agricultural labour households were in debt by 1956-57, mostly to relatives and moneylenders rather than cooperatives.

N. S. Ranganatha Rao's "The Law Of Obscenity" traces India's obscenity law to the flawed English Hicklin test, faulting it for ignoring authorial intent and judging works by isolated passages, and calls for English-style reform admitting literary-merit evidence.

Writing as "Atreya," "The Travails Of Mr. Nehru" surveys Nehru's weakened standing after the Chinese invasion, describing the Kamaraj Plan as a failed "tail-dropping" tactic and accusing Nehru of opportunistically criticising the bureaucratic planning apparatus he himself built.

Arvind A. Deshpande's piece on "The Constitution (17th Amendment) Bill" warns it will render the peasant proprietor class "almost legally extinct," paralleling Article 6 of the Soviet constitution, and predicts a further amendment extending state land claims to industrial and residential property.

K. Santhanam's reprinted "Without Comment" column warns against the "dangerous craze of nationalization" spreading across food, banking and transport, attributing much of the push to Communist strategy aimed at eliminating the independent middle class.

A review (signed V.B.K.) of A. G. Noorani's "Our Credulity and Ignorance" summarises Noorani's argument that Nehru's government was credulous toward China from 1950 to 1959, first through appeasement over Tibet and then through personal reliance on Chou En-lai.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Justice Brandeis warning that liberty's greatest danger lies in "insidious encroachment by men of zeal," and Dr. Lohia contrasting the pay of officers and labourers at the Rourkela Steel Factory.

An unsigned piece bylined "Saadi," "Bhubaneshwar -- Its Achievements And Failures," reviews the Congress's 68th Plenary socialism resolution as vaguer and more pious than its 1931 Karachi statement, crediting it with affirming labour's dignity while faulting it for evading mass poverty, bureaucratic stranglehold and corruption.

Raman Desai's "Israel And Arab States" traces the Arab-Israeli dispute to the 1922 Palestine Mandate, argues Nasser exploits anti-Israel sentiment to distract from domestic economic failure, and urges India to recognise Israel's right to exist despite its non-aligned foreign policy.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "Ministerial Corruption" criticises Nehru's selective use of Lord Denning's report to shield the Kairon affair, distinguishes political from official corruption, and calls for legislation requiring ministers to disclose personal and family assets.

S. R. Mohan Das's "New Prohibition Policy" examines Maharashtra's relaxed liquor policy under V. P. Naik, arguing prohibition has become a Gandhian "sacred cow" rather than an effective response to alcoholism, and recommends a UK-style graduated approach over blanket bans.

A. G. Noorani's "New Delhi And China" methodically documents columnist N. J. Nanporia's reversal from uncompromising toughness on China to accepting the Colombo Proposals and later downplaying the border dispute, concluding the shift reflects either lack of candour or genuine confusion.
The issue's "Without Comment" and "With Many Voices" columns round out the issue with reprinted items on the US Seventh Fleet in Asian waters and miscellaneous quotations from public figures.

V. B. Karnik's "Consensus Or Conflict?" addresses the Asoka Mehta-PSP disciplinary controversy to argue Indian democrats should prioritise building a shared civic consensus over pursuing conflict, since India lacks the entrenched consensus that lets Anglo-American democracies safely tolerate party rivalry.

Writing as "Saadi," "Danger In Kashmir" warns against restoring G. M. Sadiq to the Kashmir cabinet after the Hazratbal relic theft, tracing his political biography to argue he is a "confirmed communist" who has embedded sympathisers in Kashmir's unions, student bodies and press.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "Question Of Succession," prompted by Nehru's illness, argues non-alignment has repeatedly failed India's interests and proposes a small Supreme Emergency Council including opposition figures like Rajaji and Kripalani to manage foreign and defence policy during a transition.

M. R. Pai's "Bangalore Convention Of Swatantra Party" reports on the party's Third Convention, highlighting Masani's candid organisational report on its weak cadre and dependence on "supine" Big Business funding, and its shifting social base toward young professionals.

N. S. Ranganath Rao's continuing "The Law Of Obscenity" proposes recasting IPC Section 292 to require knowledge and intent, judge works as a whole, and admit expert evidence on literary merit, modelled partly on Britain's 1959 Obscene Publications Act.

M. A. Venkata Rao's "Tradition Looks At Marx" argues Vedic, Buddhist and Jain traditions share Marxism's concern for the poor but reject its materialism, describing a traditional dharma-based social order that ranked truth-seekers above rulers and rulers above the bourgeoisie.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Mao Tse-tung predicting the collapse of Khrushchev, "that paper tiger," and reproduces the statutory ownership statement naming Adam Adil as printer/publisher and Raman K. Desai as editor.

M. P. Chitale's "Productive Activity and Taxation" argues the 1964-65 Union Budget penalises entrepreneurship, showing corporation tax on closely-held companies rising to 54-60% and new taxes on bonus shares and dividends choking the flow of savings into equity investment.

G. L. Mehta's "Defence And Development" argues the 1962 Chinese invasion should have galvanised lasting national self-reliance rather than a fading emergency mood, criticising India's growing dependence on foreign aid, which rose from about 10% of Plan outlay in the First Plan to nearly 30% in the Third.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "Access To Government Documents" argues India needlessly borrowed Britain's 50-year secrecy rule for government records despite having no domestic Act requiring it, and calls for opening pre-1947 archives to historians before personal reminiscences are lost.

Adam Adil's "Condition Of Muslims In China" documents the abolition of Muslim waqf properties, the forced replacement of Arabic with Cyrillic script, and banned Quranic instruction under Chinese Communist rule, citing continuing armed Muslim resistance in Sinkiang and criticising Pakistan's alignment with Peking.

J. Mieroszewski's "Russia And China—A Polish View," reprinted from the Polish monthly Kultura, argues Poland's national interest favours a strong, anti-Russian China as a counterweight to Soviet imperial dominance, framing the Sino-Soviet split as a historical-territorial dispute rather than a purely ideological one.

A review signed "Junius" of C. L. Sareen's "U.S.S.R. vs. Tarasov" recounts a defecting Soviet sailor's legal battle in Indian courts, praising the magistrates' rejection of fabricated Soviet evidence as a vindication of Indian judicial independence against Soviet pressure.

Gayatri Devi's Lok Sabha speech on the "Santhanam Committee Report on Corruption" argues the Committee's recommendations do not go far enough, calling for a broad statutory definition of corruption covering influence-peddling, disclosure of ministers' assets to an independent tribunal, and confiscation of unaccounted wealth as the penalty.

M. R. Masani's Lok Sabha speech on the "Dange Letters" presses the government to authenticate the disputed 1924 letters in which CPI leader S. A. Dange purportedly offered to serve as an intelligence agent for the colonial Governor-General, accusing the Home Minister of evading the question to avoid embarrassing Nanda or antagonising the Soviet Union.

An unsigned compilation, "When Thieves Fall Out....," assembles press reports of internal CPI accusations against chairman S. A. Dange, alleging he held undisclosed property through a nominee and received substantial funds from the Soviet-aligned World Federation of Trade Unions.

K. K. Sinha's "Crisis In Eastern India" describes an accelerating refugee exodus of non-Muslims from East Pakistan following the Khulna riots, reporting 4,000-5,000 crossings a day by mid-April 1964 and the inadequacy of the Dandakaranya rehabilitation scheme.

Raman Desai's "Kashmir—Past And Future" gives a long historical account of the 1947 accession, the UN plebiscite resolution, and Sheikh Abdullah's later advocacy for independence, concluding India must resist further Pakistani pressure even at the risk of war.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari calling "Congress socialism" a "South Sea Bubble" and Jayaprakash Narayan observing that "the freedom fighters of yesterday began so early to imitate the language of the imperialists."

S. R. Mohan Das's "Prohibition and Temperance" argues Maharashtra's newly liberalised liquor policy still conflates prohibition with temperance, proposing government-run beverage-and-food stalls and a state toddy monopoly with capped alcohol content as an alternative to both rigid prohibition and outright repeal.

New Zealand Ombudsman Sir Guy Powels's "Common Justice," reprinted from The Guardian, reviews his first 18 months in office handling 1,100 complaints through informal departmental cooperation, arguing liberty today is threatened more by the "suffocation" of an expanding welfare state than by external militant ideology.

M. R. Pai's "The Food Crisis—Who Is Responsible?" blames rising food prices on inflationary deficit financing under Soviet-style planning and gross inefficiency in state grain-handling, citing Rs. 12.38 crores in state-trading losses in 1962-63 and calling for treating agriculture as an industry rather than nationalising the grain trade.

"Forecast: Cloudy, Windy" compiles quotations from Asoka Mehta warning of an annual Rs. 100-crore tax increase and observing that industrial growth has failed to trigger corresponding agricultural growth.

V. B. Karnik's "Kashmir—A Plea For Fresh Thinking," written after Sheikh Abdullah's release, disputes that the Constituent Assembly's ratification or one-party state elections constitute genuine popular endorsement of accession, and urges either full integration via abrogating Article 370 or a region-by-region ascertainment of Kashmiri popular will.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari calling India's "adventure with democracy" an "expensive disappointment" while crediting Nehru alone with securing Indo-Pak sacrifices.

Purshottam Trikamdas's memoir "Jawaharlal Nehru As I Knew Him" offers a candid, unsentimental account spanning 1917 to the mid-1950s, recalling Nehru's 1957 admission of responsibility for SEATO's formation and his troubling idolisation of V. K. Krishna Menon, while concluding "with the end of his life, an era has ended."

Y. N. Sukthankar's "Nehru The Administrator" praises Nehru's prompt, non-dictatorial working style and credits him as the intellectual force behind key features of the Five-Year Plans, closing with Churchill's remark that Nehru had "conquered the three great enemies of mankind."

Robert Conquest's "The Fog Of Peace," adapted from a BBC broadcast, argues against relaxing vigilance toward the Soviet Union even amid talk of détente, using Soviet census data to argue Stalin's purges, not just the war, explain the USSR's postwar gender imbalance.

Surendra Mohan's "Consensus Or Conformity?" rebuts V. B. Karnik's earlier article, arguing consensus and conflict are intertwined and that manufacturing artificial unity risks leaving rising social conflicts unchannelled.

Rohit Dave's "The Budget Concessions" criticises the Finance Minister's budget as ineffective against black-market lending at 18-24% interest and the Reserve Bank's restrictive credit policy, calling for a comprehensive economic strategy rather than piecemeal tinkering.

Victor Frank's "The Case Of Joseph Brodsky" recounts the Leningrad trial and internal exile of the 24-year-old poet for "parasitism," highlighting Soviet writers' unprecedented public petition on his behalf as a sign of new dissent under Khrushchev.

The closing "With Many Voices" column, reacting to Nehru's death, opens with C. Rajagopalachari's tribute in Swarajya and includes Asoka Mehta's chariot metaphor of heavy industry and agriculture as the "two wheels" of development.

Raman Desai's "South Vietnam and Ourselves" argues Communist China has spent years fomenting civil wars around South East Asia's seaboard, calls for India to abandon panchsheel neutrality, and urges Indian foreign policy to align openly with the U.S., Cambodia, Laos, Vietnam and Malaysia against China.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "After The Das Report" treats the Das Commission's findings against Punjab Chief Minister Pratap Singh Kairon as a turning point, proposing mandatory asset declarations for all political officeholders and referral of corruption findings to the President or Governors and statutory Commissions of Inquiry.

"Goldwater On Goldwater" reprints excerpts of Senator Barry Goldwater's Der Spiegel interview after his Republican nomination, in which he frames the Cold War as a struggle between "godless people and the people of God," claims Communists have broken 51 of 52 postwar agreements, and states the U.S. is already fighting "World War III... in Southeast Asia."

Raman Desai's sarcastic "Is Your Travel Necessary?" contrasts foreign-exchange privations on ordinary citizens with hospitality-funded foreign trips taken by officials like Bombay Chief Minister Naik, and calls for Indians to be allowed to retain pre-independence foreign-currency balances held abroad.

Dahyabhai V. Patel's "A Visit To Free China (June 1964)" reports on a delegation tour of South Vietnam and Taiwan, crediting Taiwan's land-reform programme with a claimed 369% rise in agricultural production since 1946 and urging Indian recognition of the Taiwan government.

V. B. Karnik reviews A. J. Fonseca's "Wage Determination and Organised Labour in India," crediting it with showing trade unions influence wage levels but exert no control over prices or employment, while noting Fonseca's inattention to wage-setting shifting from collective bargaining to tribunals.

The closing "With Many Voices" column includes Barry Goldwater's acceptance-speech line that "moderation in the pursuit of justice is no virtue" and William F. Buckley Jr.'s remark that under federal encroachment "States today are merely eunuchs."

M. R. Masani's "The Food Crisis" blames stagnant foodgrain output and rising prices on the Second Plan's priority for heavy industry over agriculture, criticises the government for scapegoating peasants and traders as hoarders, and calls for releasing buffer stocks, ending zonal restrictions and halting food exports.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's "Choosing The Leader" surveys three centuries of British prime-ministerial selection, from Walpole through the criticised 1963 "soundings" that produced Sir Alec Douglas-Home, to ask what precedent Lal Bahadur Shastri's unexpected rise offers for how Congress will choose future leaders.

N. S. Ranganath Rao opens a two-part essay, "Obscenity: Literature And Law," tracing the culturally relative history of obscenity regulation in English law from antiquity through the 1868 Hicklin test that Indian courts adopted, setting out the opposing arguments of free-expression and moral-restraint advocates.

Alexander Frater's satirical dialogue "Goulash And Ballet," reprinted from Punch, imagines Khrushchev and Mao privately coordinating a feigned Sino-Soviet rivalry for propaganda purposes while secretly planning a staged nuclear provocation.
The issue closes with "With Many Voices," a page of topical quotations from figures including President Johnson, Dean Rusk, G. L. Nanda and Asoka Mehta on world and Indian affairs.

Philip Spratt's "The Hindu Personality," delivered at the Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom's Poona seminar, argues from a Freudian perspective that the Hindu psyche is narcissistic rather than punitive, tracing this to Advaita Vedanta and indulgent child-rearing, and asks whether liberty can be made part of the ruling elite's ego-ideal.

Rohit Dave's "South East Asia And Ourselves" surveys the regional crisis in Laos, Vietnam and Malaysia after the Tonkin Gulf incident, rejecting both an all-out Indian military buildup and abandoning non-alignment for Western alliances, and calls for India to lead a regional response to Chinese expansionism.

"Russian Aid" reprints excerpts from the Chinese Communist Party's February 1964 letter to the CPSU rebutting Soviet claims of one-sided aid, detailing Chinese exports of grain and strategic minerals to the USSR and accusing Moscow of abruptly withdrawing 1,390 experts in 1960.

The "Without Comment" column reprints a Pravda article criticising the Communist Party of China for failing to hold regular Party Congresses and for the leadership deciding matters by "the directives of Mao Tse-tung" rather than its own Rules.

B. K. Desai's review of Peter Lyons's "Neutralism" argues non-alignment degenerated from a sound policy of avoiding military pacts into a dogma that blinded India to the communist threat, citing the Colombo powers' refusal to condemn Chinese aggression in 1962.

An unsigned piece, "China's Territorial Claims," documents Chinese expansionist doctrine and reproduces a 1954 Chinese textbook map showing claims on Ladakh, Nepal, Sikkim, Bhutan, NEFA/Assam and other neighbouring territories.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes C. Rajagopalachari denouncing the Fourth Plan's Rs. 22,000-crore outlay as "the nation's biggest enemy" and Sukarno describing himself as "a Communist, religious and nationalist as well."

V. B. Karnik's "Plus Ca Change--" analyses Khrushchev's October 1964 removal as a "palace revolution" engineered by a small circle of Communist Party leaders, with Kosygin taking the premiership and Brezhnev the party secretaryship, and warns a resulting Sino-Soviet rapprochement could reduce Russian willingness to support India against China.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's essay traces parliamentary privilege from Speaker Lenthall's 1642 defiance of Charles I through the Keshav Singh affair, in which the U.P. Vidhan Sabha's contempt powers clashed with the Allahabad High Court, prompting a Presidential Reference to the Supreme Court.

N. S. Ranganath Rao's second installment on "Obscenity: Literature And Law" argues India's Hicklin-derived obscenity test wrongly ignores authorial intent and judges books by isolated passages, and calls for admitting expert literary evidence as England's 1959 Obscene Publications Act does.

Raman Desai reviews A. G. Noorani's "The Kashmir Question," crediting its treatment of the U.N. Commission resolutions while criticising its disorganisation, and argues India should keep seeking agreement with Pakistan on frontier defence against China even at some sacrifice.

S. Natarajan reviews Charles H. Heimsath's "Indian Nationalism and Hindu Social Reform," praising its account of how the reform movement fed into nationalism while disputing R. C. Majumdar's thesis that 19th-century Hindus and Muslims lived in "water-tight" cultural compartments.

Leonard Schapiro reviews the anthology "Half-way to the Moon: New Writing from Russia," singling out Alexander Solzhenitsyn's "Matryona's Home" as its masterpiece and describing how Viktor Nekrasov's honest travelogue of the West reportedly led Khrushchev to suggest his expulsion from the Party.

M. R. Masani's editorial "The Bomb" argues China's atomic test is chiefly a political and psychological weapon, rejects an independent Indian nuclear deterrent as unaffordable, and urges India to seek a formal mutual-security understanding with the United States.

A. G. Mulgaonkar's essay, headed with Charles I's trial quotation, analyses the Supreme Court's advisory opinion in the Keshav Singh privilege dispute, which held that Indian legislative sovereignty, unlike Britain's, is subordinate to the Constitution and that High Courts' Article 226 jurisdiction cannot be ousted by a claim of privilege.

N. S. Ranganath Rao's third installment on "Obscenity: Literature & Law" proposes rewriting IPC Section 292 with a "taken as a whole" test, exceptions for bona fide literary and scientific work, and statutory Regional Boards with binding authority replacing the ad hoc Customs advisory panel.

A report on "Press Council" summarises an Indian Committee for Cultural Freedom seminar on the proposed Press Council Bill, including S. Natarajan's dissenting letter arguing press freedom is an internal professional responsibility that no external Council can secure.

A reader's letter to the editor defends A. G. Noorani's book "The Kashmir Question" against the journal's earlier unfavourable review, citing a favourable Observer editorial and objecting to the review's characterisation of Jayaprakash Narayan as "eccentric" for favouring a negotiated Kashmir settlement.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Marshal Chen Yi on China's bomb and Fidel Castro on capitalism versus socialism, and closes with a signed note from M. R. Masani defending the journal's stance on Kashmiri self-determination even at the risk of "temporary unpopularity."

V. B. Karnik's "A Reminder" uses the defections of young Tadjik writer Aziz Oulougzade and, earlier, Svetlana Stalin to argue that fifty years of Soviet rule have failed to deliver the liberty the Revolution promised, showing the yearning for freedom cuts across Soviet class lines.

M. R. Hazaray's "Death Of Fourth Plan" blames the Planning Commission's own "doctrinaire dogmatists" for the Fourth Plan's collapse, tracing outlays rising from Rs. 3,360 crores in the First Plan to a targeted Rs. 21,350 crores, alongside unemployment backlogs rising from 5.3 to 25 million.

"Russia From Many Angles" compiles foreign press commentary marking the Revolution's fiftieth anniversary, including Louis Fischer on Russia's nationalist turn and a New York Times catalogue of Stalin's purges of Red Army officers.

Dilip Chitre's "Creativity In Crisis: Russian Story" argues Soviet writers under persecution, from Pasternak to Sinyavsky and Voznesensky, achieve a moral and creative intensity unmatched by Western "alienated" avant-gardes, and warns Indian writers against romanticising revolutionary mythology.

S. H. Deshpande's "Equality In Soviet Life" reconstructs Soviet income distribution from Western scholarship, tracing a hierarchy from a wealthy elite of artists and top officials down to forced-labour camp inmates estimated at several million under Stalin, and finds inequality has gradually narrowed since 1957.

A reprint from U.S. News & World Report, "Russian Revolution—A Balance Sheet," tallies the Revolution's fifty-year record, crediting the USSR with rising to second in world economic output and 95% literacy while estimating war, terror and famine cost the population 80 million relative to trend.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Frank Moraes observing that "Communism is no longer a monolith" and C. Rajagopalachari on majority rule not being equivalent to democracy.

Adam Adil's "Recent National Conventions" surveys the PSP, SSP, Jan Sangh and Congress party conventions, criticising the SSP's withdrawal from the UP coalition cabinet as lawless and portraying the Congress Hyderabad plenary as a win for the party's right wing that avoided self-criticism over corruption.

M. D. Kini's "A Seminar On Liberalism" reports on a Poona seminar co-sponsored by the Indian Group of Liberal International, summarising talks by B. R. Shenoy, F. A. Mehta and others on planning's failures, and closing with M. R. Masani's argument that free economies like Taiwan and Israel grew faster than planned economies like India.

R. Srinivasan's "Liberty And Russian Revolution" traces how the Revolution's promise of freedom gave way under Lenin to Cheka terror and under Stalin to the 1937 purge that killed or exiled 70% of the Central Committee, arguing even Khrushchev's "welfare totalitarianism" left the underlying lack of freedom unaddressed.

V. B. Karnik reviews Gus Tyler's "The Labour Revolution," crediting its analysis of the American trade union movement's challenges from automation and Black workers' entry into the labour force, and its argument that unions are inherently political.

An unsigned report on the "Persecution Of Writers Under Communism" details the Soviet 'literary underground' trial sentencing Yury Galanskov to seven years' hard labour, alongside continuing concern over Sinyavsky and Daniel and Czechoslovak novelist Ladislav Mnacko's protest resignation from the Party.

The Reviews section covers A. G. Noorani's biography of President Zakir Husain, K. P. S. Menon's uncritically pro-Soviet Moscow ambassadorial diary, a U.S. Information Service booklet on the Peace Corps in India, and H. R. Pardiwala's balanced pamphlet on the Shiv Sena controversy.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Frank Moraes and other commentators from January 1968 on Communist doctrine, the Naxalbari uprising, and the Soviet writers' trials.

M. D. Kini's "One Year Of Non-Congress Governments" surveys the coalition governments across North India, singling out West Bengal's gheraos and Naxalbari violence and Kerala's contempt-of-court conviction of Chief Minister E. M. S. Namboodiripad as failures, while praising Orissa's abolition of land revenue as the sole real gain for ordinary people.

Writing as "Emdeeke," the satirical column "Of Cabbages And Kings" mocks the proliferation of Indian political parties and Bombay street politics, including Bal Thackeray's promise to have Shiv Sena "sainiks" slap litterers clean.

The unsigned "Notes" section argues United Front coalitions collapsed from internal disunity rather than Congress subversion, and defends India's acceptance of the ICJ's Rann of Kutch arbitration award against M. C. Chagla's call for rejection on political grounds.

Writing as "Atreya," "'Little Summit' In New Delhi" analyses the January 1968 meeting among Kosygin, Tito and Indira Gandhi, arguing the Tashkent Agreement had permanently shifted Kashmir diplomacy from the West to the Soviet Union.

M. R. Pai's "The Image Of The Indian Economist" argues the profession's standing has fallen through careerism and political malleability, crediting B. R. Shenoy as the sole prophetic dissenter on the Second Plan Panel of Economists.

Adam Adil's "Withdrawal Of British Forces" examines Britain's 1968 decision to pull troops from east of Suez, noting Malaysia and Singapore's moves toward a NATO-style defence pact with Australia and New Zealand to fill the vacuum.
R. Srinivasan reviews a volume on "Higher Education In India" edited by A. B. Shah, praising Edward Shils's contribution while arguing education is too important to be left solely to academics.
V. B. Patankar reviews Keith Buchanan's "The South East Asian World," highlighting its concept of Southeast Asia as a "predeveloped region" whose progress was retarded by colonialism.

Writing as "Achyut Gandhi," a review of S. Vijayanand Bharathi's "Can Indira Accept This Challenge?" credits the book as a bold, objective survey of Indian politics since Independence, singling out its critical chapter on Nehru's "unscientific" dreams.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Gulzarilal Nanda asserting that planning "never helps the peasants" and S. A. Dange threatening millowners who close mills with imprisonment.

M. R. Masani's "The Budget – A Gamble" rejects deficit financing versus taxation as a false choice, calling Bokaro a "White Elephant," comparing Hindustan Steel's poor capital efficiency against Tata Steel's, and proposing dual pricing so subsidised rations reach only the genuinely poor.

A. G. Mulgaokar's "The Speaker's Role" traces the erosion of the Speaker's impartiality to Nehru's failure to have G. V. Mavalankar resign his Congress membership, using recent Punjab and Bengal controversies over gubernatorial powers to argue Speakers cannot rule on constitutional legality.

A boxed item reproduces John Chamberlain's Freeman review of James Burnham's "The War We Are In," summarising Burnham's thesis that communists of every persuasion cooperate in practice to hasten the West's collapse despite their mutual rivalries.

"Towards Understanding Madras Politics" carries rebuttal letters from K. Vedamurthy and P. S. Sridhara Murthy defending the DMK government's rice scheme and crediting C. Rajagopalachari, not the DMK, as leader of the anti-Hindi movement, with M. D. Kini's reply maintaining his sceptical view of the DMK's substantive record.

A contributed report describes the March 1968 Warsaw student demonstrations against secret-police rule and censorship, sparked by the banning of "Dziady" and Leszek Kolakowski's expulsion from the Communist Party, and the regime's subsequent purge of twelve intellectuals.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes R. K. Narayan on "Stone Age and Glass Age" coexisting in India and Weekend Review warning India is "not many mid-term elections" from public weariness with democracy.

V. B. Karnik's "Unjust and Unfair" protests the Maharashtra government's externment order against missionary Fr. Vincent Ferrer, who ran welfare work benefiting over 10,000 Nasik-district farmers for seventeen years, arguing vague undisclosed charges of "conversions" violate natural justice.

A Special Correspondent's "Exports After UNCTAD" argues both the 1964 and 1968 UNCTAD conferences failed to resolve major trade issues, noting India's exports were just 4.5% of national income in 1966-67 against 40% for the Netherlands, and calls for developing countries to prioritise their own export promotion.

M. R. Masani's piece on the "Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty" supports India's non-nuclear stance while rebutting arguments against signing the NPT, warning that refusal would isolate India alongside Albania, Cuba and North Korea and forfeit US nuclear fuel supply and goodwill.
G. L. Mehta's tribute "Fearless Warrior Of Peace" honours the assassinated Martin Luther King, tracing his explicit debt to Gandhian satyagraha through Thoreau back to the Bhagavad Gita.

A notice announces the newly established Leslie Sawhny Programme of Training for Democracy, a five-year initiative chaired by N. A. Palkhivala with M. R. Masani as Honorary Secretary, to train political workers and party cadres in democratic principles.

An unsigned review of 1967 as "another year of cultural revolution" in China describes the PLA's emergence as the only institution able to restore order, Lin Piao's rise as Mao's presumed successor, and the sustained vilification of President Liu Shao-ch'i as "China's Khrushchev."

A review signed V.B.K. of A. R. Antulay's critique of the Mahajan Commission's Maharashtra-Mysore-Kerala boundary report argues Justice Mahajan applied inconsistent linguistic-majority standards, favouring Mysore's claim to Kasargod while denying comparable Marathi-majority claims to Belgaum.

The "Towards Understanding Madras Politics" exchange continues, with readers Vedamurthy and Sridhara Murthy defending the DMK government against M. D. Kini's earlier criticism, before the editor closes the debate for reasons of space.

A "Without Comment" item reprinted from Swarajya argues Communist parties cannot be treated as ordinary democratic parties since subversion is their "first love," and calls on the Madras and Central Congress governments to free themselves from Communist influence.
The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Philip Toynbee calling the lie "the worst feature of Soviet society" and notes posters in Calcutta calling for "armed revolution, here and now."

M. R. Pai's "Social Control Over Politicians" itemises the lavish perquisites of Union Cabinet Ministers (Rs. 17,000/month versus a Rs. 2,250 salary) against Norway's leaner system, and proposes a ten-point programme including abolishing perquisites and mandatory wealth disclosure.

Writing as "Atreya," "The Viet Nam Peace Talks" frames Hanoi's stalling over the Paris talks venue as insincere negotiating posture and attacks American liberal critics of the war, including Robert Kennedy and J. K. Galbraith, as amplifying Communist psychological warfare.

The unsigned "Notes" section argues the delay in Assam's reorganisation between hill and plains populations is dangerous, and that "Anti-Congressism" has exhausted itself given Congress's recovery in Kerala and Haryana by-elections.

Chris Cook's "Portugal At War," reprinted from Socialist Commentary, surveys Portugal's colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea, detailing 165,000 troops deployed and 42% of the 1966 budget spent, and concludes the war is unwinnable and "both wrong and harmful."

Adam Adil's "Winds Of Change In Eastern Europe" reports on Alexander Dubcek's loosening of party control in Czechoslovakia, including the country's first workers' strike under communism, while contrasting Poland's stiffening resistance to reform under Gomulka.

R. Muthuswamy's "Trends In Recent Elections" analyses Indian municipal and by-election results, finding Congress inroads into Communist strongholds in Kerala and voters increasingly evaluating parties on performance rather than ideology.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes Alexander Dubcek wanting "Marks and Spencer, not Marx and Engels" and M. R. Masani comparing Indian attitudes to other nations with Brahmin treatment of Harijans.

V. B. Karnik's "Sheikh Abdulla and Kashmir Problem" argues Abdullah has offered no concrete solution to Kashmir since his release, dismisses plebiscite or independence as impractical, and proposes free and fair elections under the Election Commission as a substitute.

M. R. Pai's "Indo-Soviet Plan Tie-Up" warns against "dovetailing" India's Five-Year Plans with Soviet planning, citing the loss-making Ranchi Heavy Engineering Corporation, mounting Bokaro Steel Plant costs, and Soviet pressure to buy uneconomical Tu-134 aircraft as cautionary examples.

S. Narasimhan's "France In Turmoil" recounts the May 1968 Sorbonne student revolt and general strike of over ninety lakh workers, describing how de Gaulle's dissolution of the National Assembly produced a Gaullist landslide framed as a choice against "totalitarian Communism."

V. B. Karnik reviews Mohammad Ayub Khan's autobiography "Friends Not Masters," correcting Indian misconceptions that Ayub Khan is a military dictator or Pakistan a theocratic state, while sharply criticising his claim that Indian leaders harbour "a deep hatred for the Muslims."

Writing as "Atreya," a report on Indira Gandhi's May 1968 tour of Singapore, Australia, New Zealand and Malaysia describes her cautious avoidance of filling the vacuum left by British defence withdrawal, and Peking Radio's denunciation of the tour as an anti-China plot.

The closing "With Many Voices" column quotes M. R. Masani stating there is "too much politics in India and too little citizenship" and Nirlep Kaur's six-step prescription for transforming India into a foodgrain exporter.
